strengths: Introduces GUARD, a clear inference-time framework that combines repulsion from the memorized conditional prediction with attraction to a safer positive target, and provides a concrete instantiation based on dynamic cross-attention spike detection and attenuation.

Provides a useful empirical analysis of cross-attention distributions for verbatim versus template memorization, showing that EOT-only attenuation is insufficient and that EOT behavior differs across memorization types.
Conducts a broad empirical study across Stable Diffusion v1.4 and v2.0, verbatim and template memorization, with SSCD, CLIP, FID, ablations over blocks/heads/timesteps, and runtime comparisons.

The proposed CA attenuation alone improves over the closest prior CA-based method (Ren et al.) in several settings, and CA-in-GUARD often yields strong SSCD and quality trade-offs, especially for template memorization on SD v2.0.
Discusses limitations and ethics, including the inability of inference-time methods to erase memorized information under white-box threat models.
weaknesses: The main evaluation selects the best hyperparameter configuration per method and per metric on the same evaluation prompts, without a held-out validation split. This oracle-style selection inflates results and makes comparisons across methods with different hyperparameter ranges unreliable.

Central claims are overstated. For SD v1.4 template memorization under best-SSCD selection, Han et al. achieves lower SSCD (0.479) than CA-in-GUARD (0.517); under best-CLIP selection, Han et al. also has slightly better SSCD (0.662 vs. 0.667). Thus claims that the method is state-of-the-art across both architectures and memorization types, or that it 'dominates across settings,' are not fully supported.

The 'surgical' characterization is questionable. For SD v1.4 verbatim memorization, the searched threshold range is τ ∈ [0.01, 0.05], which would flag most tokens rather than statistical outliers, and the ablations find that attenuating all heads is stronger than restricting to hot heads for verbatim memorization. In some settings the method may behave more like broad attention scaling than surgical attenuation.
Reproducibility is weakened by the missing code link ('Code ... available at:' is blank) and by not reporting the exact best hyperparameters per setting, only search ranges.

Evaluation uses small filtered prompt sets (72, 143, and 96 prompts) with four generations per prompt; FID is reported without confidence intervals and uses only 10,000 reference images, making quality comparisons potentially noisy.

GUARD's repulsion term is not isolated. There is no ablation of repulsion alone (without CA attenuation) or comparison to standard negative-prompt guidance, while CA attenuation alone already achieves most of the reported gains. The claimed synergy between repulsion and attraction is therefore not fully demonstrated.

Some reported trade-offs are marginal or unfavorable relative to the abstract's claims: CA-in-GUARD has lower CLIP than CA attenuation in SD v1.4 verbatim memorization, identical SSCD to CA attenuation in SD v2.0 template memorization, and does not consistently improve both memorization and quality simultaneously.

strengths: The empirical analysis of cross-attention distributions distinguishing verbatim vs. template memorization is a genuine and useful diagnostic contribution: Figure 1 shows that EOT attention is *not* uniformly elevated in template memorization (indeed lower early on), which plausibly explains why the hardcoded EOT/padding attenuation of Ren et al. (2024) fails in that setting. This is a real insight that advances understanding beyond prior work.

The per-prompt statistical spike detector (Z-score outlier analysis over max token attention, with attenuation of logits prior to softmax) is a simple, principled, and dynamic alternative to hardcoded attention redistribution, and Section A.3 provides a useful robustness check showing CA attenuation does not harm non-memorized prompts.

The evaluation is broad in scope: two SD architectures (v1.4/v2.0), two memorization types, multiple strong baselines (RTA, Wen, Ren, Han), ablations on U-Net blocks/heads/timesteps, an alternative 'semantic' positive target, and a wall-clock efficiency comparison.

The paper includes an honest limitations section acknowledging that inference-time methods cannot protect against white-box/weight-access threat models, and does not overclaim in that specific respect.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is methodologically problematic and undermines the central SOTA claim. Hyperparameters are tuned on the *same* prompts used for evaluation, and the paper then reports 'the best results for each method in terms of SSCD, CLIP, and FID' with a different configuration chosen per metric. There is no held-out validation set, so the reported numbers are the minimum/maximum over a hyperparameter grid on the test set — a form of test-set selection that inflates and biases comparisons across methods and makes the head-to-head ranking unreliable.

The headline claim that CA-in-GUARD 'dominates across settings' is contradicted by the paper's own Table 1: for SD v1.4 template memorization, Han et al. (2025) achieves SSCD 0.479 vs. CA-in-GUARD's 0.517 (Han is better), and for SD v2.0 template memorization CA-in-GUARD ties CA attenuation exactly (0.193 ± 0.014 in both). The narrative overstates robustness relative to the evidence.

Gains are frequently marginal and within overlapping confidence intervals (e.g., SD v1.4 template: CA attenuation 0.530 ± 0.038 vs. CA-in-GUARD 0.517 ± 0.038; SD v2.0 template: identical 0.193). The 'attraction' term's contribution is inconsistent — in Table 4(b) CA-in-GUARD and CA attenuation are numerically identical (0.206/0.299/168.356) — suggesting the framework's second component adds little beyond the CA-attenuation special case (r=0).

Conceptual novelty of the GUARD framework is limited. Adding a repulsion term (negative weight on the conditional prediction) plus an attraction term to classifier-free guidance closely resembles existing negative-prompting/contrastive-guidance formulations, and the concrete instantiation is an incremental modification of Ren et al. (2024) (statistical spike detection replacing hardcoded EOT/padding).

The efficiency claim that the three batched U-Net evaluations yield 'efficiency close to that of a single forward pass' is misleading: batching improves GPU utilization but does not reduce FLOPs, and Table 5 shows ~45% wall-clock overhead (e.g., 789s vs. 543s baseline for SD v1.4 verbatim).

After filtering to SSCD > 0.7, the evaluation sets are small (72/143/96 prompts), giving limited statistical power and noisy FID values computed against a 10k-image LAION reference; FID on a few hundred generations is a weak quality signal.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the code link is empty ('The code for reproducing the results is available at:' with nothing following), and there are reference inconsistencies (Han et al. listed as 2023 in the bibliography but cited as 2025).

No qualitative generated-image examples are shown. For a memorization-mitigation paper, visual before/after examples (memorized original vs. mitigated generation) are important and their absence weakens the evidential case.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and practical problem: inference-time memorization mitigation for text-to-image diffusion models. It avoids retraining or finetuning and is therefore attractive for deployed pretrained models.

The empirical analysis of cross-attention patterns is a useful contribution. It shows that EOT-only attenuation is insufficient and that verbatim and template memorization exhibit different cross-attention signatures, motivating dynamic per-prompt intervention.

The proposed GUARD framework is simple and conceptually clean: it modifies classifier-free guidance by combining repulsion from the memorized conditional prediction with attraction toward a safer target. The CA-in-GUARD instantiation is a reasonable and well-motivated choice of positive target.

The evaluation is broad within its scope: two Stable Diffusion architectures, verbatim and template memorization, SSCD/CLIP/FID metrics, several baselines, and ablations over U-Net blocks, heads, timesteps, and alternative attract components.

The method appears to improve memorization mitigation over prior inference-time baselines, especially for template memorization and SD v2.0, and the paper also studies trade-offs through Pareto-style analyses rather than reporting only one operating point.
The robustness check on non-memorized prompts is valuable: it suggests CA attenuation can be applied without needing to know in advance whether a prompt is memorized, which is practically important.

The limitations and impact discussion is honest. The authors correctly acknowledge that inference-time mitigation does not erase memorized information from weights and cannot protect against white-box extraction.
Implementation details are mostly well documented, including hardware, inference steps, hyperparameter ranges, and batching strategy, which helps reproducibility.
weaknesses: The experimental scope is limited to SD v1.4 and SD v2.0 with filtered subsets of the Webster memorized-prompt set. The filtered evaluation sets are relatively small (72, 143, and 96 prompts), and there is no evidence on newer architectures such as SDXL, SD3, or DiT-based text-to-image models.

Comparison fairness is not fully established. The paper tunes hyperparameters per architecture and memorization type, but the search ranges for baseline methods are not given, and selecting the best configuration per metric individually can overstate each method's practical performance and may favor methods with more hyperparameters.

The improvement of CA-in-GUARD over CA attenuation alone is often small and sometimes statistically ambiguous. For example, in Table 1 SD v2.0 template memorization has identical SSCD (0.193 ± 0.014) for both, and CLIP is slightly lower for CA-in-GUARD; the claim of improving or maintaining every metric in every setting is stronger than the evidence shown.

FID is computed on relatively small generated sets against a 10k-image LAION reference, without confidence intervals. The resulting FID values are very high and may be noisy, making the quality comparisons less convincing than the SSCD comparisons.

The spike detector uses a max-attention z-score with a threshold tau that varies widely across settings ([0.01, 0.05] for SD v1.4 verbatim versus [0.5, 3.0] for template memorization). This suggests the detector is sensitive to setting-specific tuning, and the paper does not provide a sensitivity analysis or theoretical justification for the chosen statistic.

Efficiency claims are somewhat overstated. Table 5 shows CA-in-GUARD adds roughly 40–45% wall-clock overhead over no mitigation, which is moderate rather than minimal, even if it remains faster than some baselines.

Reproducibility is weakened by the missing code URL in the manuscript ('available at:' is blank) and by incomplete details for baseline hyperparameter tuning. Some presentation issues also remain, such as inconsistent citation years and minor typographical errors.

The comparison is limited to a small set of prior inference-time methods. The claim of being 'by far the most robust' method is bounded by these baselines and settings and does not establish superiority over all relevant mitigation approaches.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: inference-time mitigation of memorization in text-to-image diffusion models, with practical advantages over training-time and finetuning-time unlearning.
Provides a useful empirical analysis of cross-attention patterns for verbatim vs. template memorization, showing that EOT-only attenuation is insufficient and motivating dynamic per-prompt detection.
Proposes GUARD, a clear contrastive guidance framework, and a concrete instantiation CA-in-GUARD with a statistical spike detector and surgical logit attenuation.

Evaluation is broad: multiple SD architectures (v1.4, v2.0, v3.0), verbatim and template memorization, SSCD/CLIP/FID/DINO metrics, multiple baselines, confidence intervals, qualitative examples, and ablations over blocks, heads, timesteps, samplers, steps, and CFG scales.
Includes robustness checks on non-memorized prompts and a full-spectrum evaluation over all 500 memorized examples, which partially addresses concerns about filtering high-SSCD examples.
The limitations section is honest about the fundamental limitation of inference-time methods: they do not erase memorized information from weights and do not protect against white-box adversaries.
The method is computationally lighter than several baselines and can batch the three required forward passes, keeping memory usage close to standard generation.
Presentation is generally clear, with informative diagrams and well-organized appendix experiments.
weaknesses: The central claim of consistent state-of-the-art performance is contradicted by the paper's own results. In Table 1, for SD v1.4 template memorization, Han et al. achieves better SSCD (0.479 vs. 0.517) and also better CLIP/FID than CA-in-GUARD. In Table 5b (best CLIP), CA-in-GUARD's SSCD is worse than Ren et al., Wen et al., and Han et al. for SD v1.4 template memorization, despite the text claiming CA-in-GUARD 'by far improves' SSCD even when configuring for best CLIP. The abstract and conclusion overstate the robustness and SOTA status.

The GUARD repulsion term may largely reduce to lowering the effective classifier-free guidance scale. Eq. 5 can be rewritten as eps_phi + (s-r)(eps^- - eps_phi) + s(eps^+ - eps^-), so the negative-target term directly scales down the standard conditional direction. Since lower CFG is a known simple way to reduce memorization, a tuned lower-CFG baseline under the same quality constraint is essential to attribute gains to GUARD rather than to reduced guidance strength. The current CFG-scale ablation does not serve as this baseline.

The hyperparameter selection protocol is not fully transparent or clearly symmetric. The paper grid-searches its own tau, alpha, and r per setting but does not report the search ranges or selection procedure for the baselines. This makes it difficult to verify that all methods received comparable tuning effort.

The spike detector's threshold tau varies by orders of magnitude across settings (e.g., 0.01-0.05 for SD v1.4 verbatim vs. 0.5-3.0 for template), inconsistent with the stated example tau=3. This suggests the detector is highly setting-specific and may not be as robust or automatic as claimed, and it undercuts the 'surgical' framing.

The method attenuates all heads in selected mid/down blocks by default, so the intervention is less surgical than the title and framing imply. The head ablation shows restricting to top-k heads is insufficient for verbatim memorization, which is a useful finding but weakens the precision claim.

The efficiency claim that the method is 'close to a single forward pass' is somewhat overstated: Table 8 shows CA-in-GUARD takes about 10.96s vs. 7.58s for no mitigation on SD v1.4, roughly a 45% runtime overhead, even if memory usage is similar.

Reproducibility is weakened by a blank code URL in the manuscript and incomplete reporting of baseline hyperparameters/implementation details. While anonymity may explain the missing link, no anonymized repository is provided.

The filtered evaluation uses relatively small subsets (72, 143, and 96 prompts), and FID values are very high (150-300), making image-quality comparisons harder to interpret. The full-spectrum results help, but the main conclusions rely heavily on the filtered high-SSCD subset.

Some claims about template memorization being consistently better mitigated by CA-in-GUARD are not supported across all settings; the paper would benefit from more careful, setting-specific claims and a clear discussion of where and why Han et al. remains stronger.

strengths: The empirical analysis in Section 5.1 distinguishing verbatim from template memorization is genuinely useful: showing that EOT cross-attention is elevated for memorized verbatim prompts but not (and even depressed early) for template memorization is a concrete, non-obvious insight that explains why Ren et al.'s EOT-attenuation fails on template memorization.

The dynamic, per-prompt spike detector is a sensible step beyond hard-coded EOT/BOT attenuation, and the overall design (detect statistical outliers in cross-attention, attenuate their logits) is clean and easy to implement.

The evaluation is broad in coverage: three SD architectures, two memorization types, ablations over U-Net blocks, heads, timesteps, samplers, step counts, guidance schedules and CFG scales, plus a DINO-based retrieval check and an efficiency/memory analysis (Tables 6–9, Figs. 8–11). The batched forward-pass implementation (A.2) is a practical plus.
Section A.3's check on non-memorized prompts (no measurable quality/SSCD change) is a valuable robustness result that relaxes a common assumption in the literature.
The Limitations section (A.1) is honest about the inability of inference-time methods to protect against white-box weight access.
weaknesses: Novelty is modest. GUARD's 'attractive-repulsive' guidance is essentially a repulsion term (a form of negative guidance) combined with an attention-attenuation target that is closely related to Ren et al. (2024). The 'novel statistical mechanism' for detection is a Z-score outlier test on per-token maximum attention mass—a standard heuristic, not a principled detector.

The central framework contribution (GUARD's repulsion term) is not clearly validated. In several best configurations the results for CA-in-GUARD are numerically identical to plain CA attenuation (e.g., SD v2.0 template SSCD 0.193 vs 0.193; SD v1.4 verbatim best-CLIP row 0.206/0.299/168.356 identical in Table 5b). This strongly suggests the selected best configuration has r≈0, i.e., GUARD collapses to the base CA-attenuation method, so the paper's headline 'framework' claim is under-supported.

The claim that CA-in-GUARD 'dominates across settings' is contradicted by the paper's own Table 1: for SD v1.4 template memorization Han et al. achieves SSCD 0.479 versus 0.517 for CA-in-GUARD, i.e., a prior method is better on the primary metric. The 'by far the most consistent method' framing overstates the evidence.

Hyperparameter sensitivity undermines the 'principled/automatic' framing: the detection threshold tau ranges from 0.01–0.05 for verbatim to 0.5–3.0 for template memorization (Table 2), spanning two orders of magnitude, and the quality budget is applied per setting. This suggests the detector is fragile and heavily tuned per setting rather than robust.

Evaluation protocol issues. (a) The per-metric, per-method hyperparameter selection in Figure 3 (best SSCD / best CLIP / best FID chosen with different configurations) makes cross-method comparison hard to interpret and is somewhat cherry-picked. (b) The reported 95% CIs are computed across the four generations per prompt, not across prompts, so they do not reflect prompt-level variability and are likely too narrow for the claims made. (c) Filtering to SSCD>0.7 (72–143 prompts per setting, 4 images each) yields a small evaluation set and re-defines the benchmark relative to prior work, complicating direct comparison to published numbers.

FID is computed between generated images and a LAION reference set, producing values of ~150–300 (Tables 1, 5, 7). These are far outside the usual FID range and are not comparable to standard benchmarks, which makes the 'quality preserved' claims difficult to calibrate.

Missing obvious baseline: simple negative-prompting / CFG-with-negative-target guidance is not compared, so it is unclear how much GUARD's repulsion adds over a trivial negative-guidance baseline that any practitioner could implement.

The title/framing ('You Don't Need All That Attention', 'surgical') is at odds with the paper's own ablation (A.5.2), which finds that attenuating all heads in the selected blocks is the strongest default and that head-selective attenuation is insufficient for verbatim memorization.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: inference-time memorization mitigation in text-to-image diffusion models, avoiding costly retraining or finetuning while reducing privacy/copyright risks.

Provides useful empirical analysis of cross-attention distributions, showing that EOT-only attenuation is insufficient and that verbatim vs. template memorization exhibit different attention patterns; this motivates a dynamic per-prompt intervention.

Introduces GUARD, a contrastive guidance framework combining repulsion from the standard conditional prediction with attraction toward a safer positive target, and instantiates it with a novel CA-spike detector plus surgical logit attenuation.

Evaluation is broad: SD v1.4, v2.0, and v3.0; verbatim and template memorization; multiple baselines; SSCD, CLIP, FID, and DINO metrics; ablations over blocks, heads, timesteps, samplers, steps, and CFG scales; qualitative examples and efficiency measurements.
CA attenuation alone improves over the closely related Ren et al. baseline in several settings, and CA-in-GUARD often achieves the best or competitive SSCD while maintaining reasonable quality.
The limitations section honestly acknowledges that inference-time methods do not erase memorized information from weights and cannot protect against white-box adversaries.
weaknesses: The hyperparameter selection protocol is a major concern: the paper grid-searches method-specific hyperparameters per architecture/memorization setting and then reports the best configuration for each metric (SSCD, CLIP, FID), apparently using the same evaluation data. Without a clear held-out validation split, this is oracle tuning on the test set and can overstate performance, especially for methods with more hyperparameters such as CA-in-GUARD (which adds r).

Several claims are overstated. The abstract and main text imply CA-in-GUARD consistently achieves state-of-the-art results across settings, but Table 1 shows Han et al. achieves lower SSCD (0.479 vs. 0.517) for SD v1.4 template memorization, and CA-in-GUARD is not best on all quality metrics (e.g., SD v2.0 template FID 212.7 vs. Wen et al. 188.9). Exceptions are acknowledged mainly in the appendix, while the main narrative is stronger than the evidence supports.

The technical novelty is moderate: GUARD's Eq. (5) is a variant of contrastive/negative classifier-free guidance, and the spike detector is simple z-score thresholding of maximum attention mass. There is limited theoretical grounding for why these statistical outliers correspond to memorization-critical tokens or why attenuation should preserve semantic alignment.

Reproducibility is weakened by the missing code URL in the manuscript, and the exact selected hyperparameters for each method/setting are not fully tabulated. The custom filtering (SSCD > 0.7) and per-metric tuning protocol also make exact reproduction and fair comparison harder.

The statistical evaluation is not fully convincing: confidence intervals are reported across four generations per prompt rather than across prompts, and FID is computed over relatively small generated sets with a LAION reference, which may be unstable. The main evaluation focuses on highly memorized examples, with full-spectrum results only in the appendix.

The threat model is limited to black-box inference-time mitigation. The paper does not evaluate robustness against adaptive adversaries or extraction attacks, and the impact statement remains high-level despite the privacy/copyright framing.
